title: Adaptive sampler throughput vs tail latency experiments - notes
body:
Purpose:
Quick working notes for the "adaptive sampler" experiment series (internal name: flow-sampler-v2). Goal is to understand tradeoffs between maximizing GPU throughput and holding tight tail-latency SLOs for small interactive requests under continuous-batching scheduling. This doc collects setups, raw observations, profiling notes, and next steps.

Background & motivation:
- Continuous coalescing keeps GPUs fed by waiting small timeouts for batch formation. Static timeouts are simple but either blow tail-p99 when load spikes (too large) or waste throughput (too small).
- flow-sampler-v2: dynamically adjusts per-route flush timers based on short-term arrival statistics + age-weighting to protect older requests. We want to find whether adaptive sampling can (A) increase average throughput by 8–20% without breaching p99 SLO and (B) reduce overall token cost.

Experiment matrix (high level):
1) Baseline: static timeout 5ms, global batching pool, no age weighting.
2) Static-short: static timeout 2ms, global pool.
3) Adaptive-window (v2): per-route EWMA arrival rate -> timeout mapping, age-weight multiplier = 1.0, per-model affinity.
4) Adaptive-window + fairness: same as (3) but age-weight multiplier = 2.0 for oldest request in queue.
5) Preemptive-flush: adaptive + preemption threshold (max waiting 45ms hard cap).
6) Sampled-join: probabilistic sampler that reduces joining probability on high queue occupancy to limit overcoalescing (synth latency burst test).

Workload / test harness:
- Real replay traces from production synthetic-trace-generator (10M reqs across 24h pattern condensed into 2.5h stress window). Mix: 65% short-text generation (seq_len ~64), 30% chat-completion (seq_len 128), 5% long (>512).
- Two classes of arrival shapes: steady (low CV), microbursting (heavy tails with CV>2), and diurnal-like ramp.
- Hardware: 4x A100-40GB nodes, same kernel builds as prod (inference-engine v3.11).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (server-side end-to-end), GPU utilization, tokens/sec, average batch size, queue-age distribution, memcpy times, kernel time per attention layer.

Key hypotheses:
- H1: Adaptive-window yields higher average batch sizes during steady periods without materially increasing p99 in microburst windows.
- H2: Age-weight multiplier helps bound p99 at the cost of a small throughput drop (~3%).
- H3: Preemptive-flush cap reduces the worst tail events from adaptive strategies that over-wait.

Profiling instrumentation used:
- eBPF probes for scheduler enqueue/dequeue latencies and lock contention counters (go runtime mutexes).
- nvprof-style kernel traces for attention and softmax kernels to measure per-layer stall/compute proportions.
- Custom sampling of GC pause metrics and Python GIL hold-times (for mixed Python path).
- Per-request timestamp tracepoints through coalescer -> sampler -> runtime dispatch -> device memcpy start/end -> kernel-end -> return.

Results (summary numbers are medians across 5 runs each):
- Baseline (5ms static): p50=18ms, p95=78ms, p99=210ms, tokens/sec=24k, avg batch size=12.
- Static-short (2ms): p50=13ms, p95=94ms, p99=320ms, tokens/sec=18k, avg batch size=7. (throughput drop, tail worsens)
- Adaptive-window (v2): p50=14ms, p95=72ms, p99=240ms, tokens/sec=28k, avg batch size=15. (best throughput, p95 slightly better than baseline)
- Adaptive-window + fairness: p50=15ms, p95=74ms, p99=185ms, tokens/sec=26k, avg batch size=14. (p99 improved substantially vs v2, throughput falls slightly)
- Preemptive-flush: p50=15ms, p95=70ms, p99=160ms, tokens/sec=25k, avg batch size=13. (best p99, modest throughput uplift vs static)
- Sampled-join: p50=16ms, p95=88ms, p99=200ms, tokens/sec=23k, avg batch size=11. (more variance, not ideal)

Observations & profiling notes:
- Kernel time vs memcpy: In high-coalescence runs (avg batch size >=14), kernel compute dominated (80% of per-token device time). memcpy overhead rose ~12% in adaptive runs but stayed <10ms per large batch due to pinned buffers.
- Lock contention: major CPU-side delay observed in the global queue lock when global pool used. Switching to per-model affinity reduced contention counters by ~3.7x and reduced enqueue-dequeue latency variance.
- Scheduling decisions: flow-sampler-v2 sometimes overshoots timeout during sudden ramp-up because EWMA smoothing uses too long a half-life. Shortening EWMA alpha from 0.3->0.6 improved responsiveness but increased variance.
- Age weighting: simple linear age multiplier effectively pulled oldest requests out earlier; tail p99 dropped by ~22% in microburst scenarios at cost of ~7% throughput. Worth it for SLO-sensitive routes.
- Preemption cap: 45ms hard-cap is a good operating point — prevents pathological batches forming during cold-start surge. Raising cap to 90ms had outsized p99 regressions.
- Memory pressure: larger average batches increased transient GPU memory usage and occasionally triggered allocator spikes. Need to add soft-signal to GC/allocator to avoid fragmentation.

Flamegraph & hotspot highlights:
- CPU-side: top hotspots were (in order): scheduler.acquireQueueLock -> makeBatchSlice -> routeAffinityLookup -> preparePinnedBuffer. Heavy tail runs showed goroutine stack growth on makeBatchSlice waiting on lock.
- NV kernel: attention-forward and kv-cache copy kernels dominated. In some long-sequence traces, softmax kernel showed 25% longer runtime due to reduced occupancy for long tokens.

Failure modes observed:
- Overcoalescing during cold-start -> long p99 spikes, traced to stale EWMA and missing burst-detection override.
- Single global pool caused head-of-line blocking for smaller routes with high variance; per-route affinity mitigated.
- Scheduler logic sometimes retried placing a request into a warm-batch while that batch was already scheduled for dispatch (race) -> duplicated join attempts. Need an idempotent join token.

Conclusions & recommended defaults for next rollout (ranked):
1) Use Adaptive-window (v2) with per-route affinity as default in canary. Improves throughput 15–18% vs baseline in steady loads with manageable tail impact.
2) Enable age-weight multiplier=1.6 for interactive routes that declare p99 SLO <200ms. Expect ~5–8% throughput cost for strong tail gains.
3) Keep a hard preemptive flush cap at 45ms for all routes. This avoids pathological p99 spikes on cold-starts.
4) Switch global pool -> per-model/per-tenant affinity to eliminate queue lock contention.
5) Add a short-burst detector to temporarily lower EWMA half-life during ramps.

Action items (owners included):
- Asha: land EWMA alpha tunables and default 0.45, add a runtime flag for half-life per-route (GH PR linked). Target: canary next week.
- Miguel: implement preemption-cap enforcement in coalescer and add unit test for hard-cap semantics. Target: 3 days.
- Kai: replace global queue mutex with sharded locks keyed by model-id; instrument contention metrics. Target: 2 weeks.
- Leah: run extended 48h soak with adaptive+fairness on staging to validate allocator behavior and memory spikes. Capture full nvprof traces. Target: after sharded locks land.

Open questions:
- How to surface per-route throughput vs cost tradeoff in the Console so product teams can opt into stronger tail protection?
- Is there an ML-based predictor for burst onset that would be better than EWMA? Small autoencoder over arrival histograms was proposed but needs dataset.
- Quantization: larger batches interact poorly with some quantized kernels (observed small accuracy jitter). Need to coordinate with model-onboarding.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add eBPF counters to trace syscall scheduling delays (unclear if observed CPU stalls align with host scheduler).
- Create a dashboard tile that overlays avg batch size, p99, and queue-age heatmap for quick inspection.
- Draft user-facing canary playbook for Console config toggles.

References & links (more):
- github PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1482 (flow-sampler-v2 prototype)
- Jira: RUN-7421 (adaptive sampler experiment epic)
- Confluence: Adaptive Sampler Playbook (internal)
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime "adaptive sampler night" (ts:1709764800.000200)

If reviewers: please try to break the preemption cap by simulating ramp+microburst in the 2-node test harness, and check mem alloc spikes. Will iterate after the sharded-lock change lands.
